title: Fed Governor Cook Signals Readiness to Raise Rates as Inflation Risks Mount
excerpt: Cook's hawkish warning joins a growing chorus at the Federal Reserve, setting up a potential clash with Chairman Warsh and the White House over the direction of interest rates.
body:
• Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook said she is "prepared to act" with a rate hike if inflation does not begin to slow, marking the most explicit hawkish signal yet from Fed leadership.
  • U.S. inflation has risen to 4.2% over the past 12 months — a three-year high — driven by the Iran war, AI-related investment, and lingering tariff effects.
  • The current federal funds rate stands at 3.50%-3.75%, and markets now expect a possible hike as early as this fall.
  • The hawkish shift creates a potential clash with Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom President Trump appointed expecting rate cuts.

Cook Breaks Ranks

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook delivered her clearest warning yet that interest rates may need to rise, telling the Exchequer Club of Washington, D.C. that she sees "a notable shift in the balance of risks relative to a year or so ago, with inflation risks now outweighing employment risks."

"If we do not see signs of disinflation soon, I am prepared to act," Cook said, according to Reuters. "I am fully committed to reaching our inflation target, and this commitment is unwavering."

Cook's remarks followed a separate speech at Stanford's Institute for Economic Policy Research where she had first signaled her willingness to raise rates, calling inflation "clearly moving in the wrong direction." The consistency of the message across multiple appearances underscores how seriously she views the risk.

"If we do not see signs of disinflation soon, I am prepared to act. I am fully committed to reaching our inflation target, and this commitment is unwavering."

— Lisa Cook, Federal Reserve Governor

What Is Driving Inflation

Three forces are pushing prices higher simultaneously. Energy costs have surged since the February 28 start of the U.S.-Iran conflict, feeding through to transportation and manufacturing. Tariffs imposed last year continue to raise import prices across consumer goods. And the artificial intelligence investment boom — with its voracious demand for chips, data center construction, and skilled labor — is creating upward pressure on both wages and materials costs.

The combination has pushed the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, to 3.8% year-over-year in April, well above the 2% target the central bank has now missed for five consecutive years. A June consumer price report did show the first monthly decline in prices in six years, but Cook cautioned that a single data point is not enough to change the trajectory.

A Growing Hawkish Chorus

Cook is not alone. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said separately that the central bank may need to act unless there is "consistent evidence of slower inflation in coming months." St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem laid out scenarios requiring a rate hike, warning that "if we don't see disinflation in the next one to two quarters, that would concern me." New York Fed President John Williams reiterated that persistently high inflation would call for higher rates.

The growing consensus creates an awkward dynamic for Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who took the job with President Trump's explicit expectation that he would lower rates. Warsh has suggested he could support a cut if paired with balance sheet reduction, and has argued that AI will help drive down inflation — a view that supports lower rates. But the data has been moving against him.

What This Means for Markets and Investors

A rate hike would be the first since 2023 and would reverse the easing cycle that markets had been pricing in. For NRI investors with exposure to U.S. equities, the implications are significant: higher rates tend to compress stock valuations, particularly in rate-sensitive sectors like technology and real estate. The S&P 500, Nasdaq, and Dow have all hit record highs in recent weeks, potentially making them vulnerable to a hawkish surprise.

Indian markets would feel the ripple effects through capital flows. Higher U.S. rates typically strengthen the dollar against the rupee and pull foreign portfolio investment out of emerging markets. The Reserve Bank of India, which held its own policy rate at 5.25% in its most recent meeting, would face additional pressure to maintain the interest rate differential.

For now, the Fed's next policy meeting on July 28-29 will offer the first real test of whether Warsh can hold together a committee that appears increasingly ready to tighten.
